--- title: "Statistics is Awesome!" subtitle: "CRJU 705 · Session 1 · Fall 2026" author: "Scott M. Mourtgos" format: revealjs: slide-number: true preview-links: auto chalkboard: true footer: "CRJU 705 · Session 1" theme: [default, custom-slides.scss] fig-align: center execute: echo: true warning: false message: false --- # Welcome {background-color="#73000A"} ## Class Introductions - Name - Place in program - Area of interest - Experience with statistics (*anxiety* about statistics?) - Why are you here? - Future plans / goals # A City Under Siege {background-color="#1B2A4A"} ## The Situation Over three months, **40 bank robberies** strike across a city's five zones: North, South, East, West, and Downtown. ::: incremental - No clear pattern. No suspects. No leads. - The robber hits banks, disappears, and resurfaces days later in a different part of the city. - Detectives are stumped. The media is escalating. Public concern is growing. - Then someone makes a call to the PD's new crime analyst team: ::: . . . > "Can you help us predict where they'll hit next?" ## What Does the Data Look Like? 40 bank robberies across 5 city zones over several months: | Variable | Meaning | |----------|---------| | `robbery_id` | Robbery sequence | | `date` | When the robbery occurred | | `zone` | Which part of the city was hit | | `day_of_year` | Numeric version of the date (for modeling time) | | `lat` & `lon` | Spatial location (for mapping) | | `prior_robberies_in_zone` | How many robberies already happened in that zone? | ## Before We Model, We Look Very little information is available: no suspect descriptions, no MO patterns — just **when** and **where**. Can we use this simple dataset to build a predictive model with statistics? . . . But before we even build a model, we can use basic plots to spot patterns. **Good data analysts always visualize before they model.** ## Timeline of Robberies by Zone — any patterns? ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](week-01-stats-is-awesome_files/figure-revealjs/timeline-plot-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Watching It Unfold Over Time ## Mapped Locations — any patterns? ## Building a Predictive Model We want to predict **where the next robbery will occur** within a short time window, based on patterns in *time*, *location*, and *prior activity*. **Key predictors:** - Day of year (captures seasonal or other unobserved time patterns) - Prior robberies in the same zone - Zone ## What Are We Trying to Predict? We use **logistic regression** to predict whether the same zone will be hit again within 10 days: - **Outcome:** `future_hit` = 1 if another robbery occurs in the *same zone* within the next 10 days; otherwise 0 - This creates a **binary classification** problem *(Don't worry about the machinery today — logistic regression is Session 12. This is a preview of where we're headed.)* ## Logistic Regression Results ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| |:-----------------------|--------:|---------:|---------:|-------:| |scale(day_of_year) | 0.034| 1.055| 0.032| 0.975| |prior_robberies_in_zone | -0.033| 0.194| -0.171| 0.864| |zoneNorth | -17.528| 3956.181| -0.004| 0.996| |zoneSouth | -17.563| 2284.020| -0.008| 0.994| |zoneEast | -1.309| 1.328| -0.986| 0.324| |zoneWest | 1.114| 2.053| 0.543| 0.587| |zoneDowntown | -0.979| 1.149| -0.852| 0.394| ::: ::: ## Predicted Risk by Zone ## Predicted Risk by Zone Based on the model, the **West Zone** has the highest likelihood of being targeted next. . . . **So what should we do with the information derived from the model?** ## Strategic Deployment :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="62%"} ::: ::: {.column width="38%"}
- 📍 **Where:** West Zone had the highest predicted probability - 🚔 **Action:** Deploy units there for surveillance and hopeful capture - 🎯 **Goal:** Increase arrest probability ::: :::: ## Case Study Wrap-Up & Discussion **Outcome:** Within days, officers apprehended the suspect in the predicted area as he was approaching a bank. Statistics turned scattered crime data into a clear lead — saving time, resources, and preventing further victimization. ::: incremental - What data did we *not* use? How could we update this model as new robberies occur in real time? - What are the risks of over-relying on a model? How do we communicate uncertainty to decision-makers? - What other areas that interest you could statistics be applied to? ::: # Course Structure {background-color="#73000A"} ## How This Course Works Everything lives on the course website — bookmark it: **** - **[Schedule](https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/schedule.html)** — topics, readings, slides, labs, homework for every session - **[Syllabus](https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/syllabus.html)** — walk-through now (grading, policies, AI policy, the mid-term warning) - **Two textbooks:** Stanton (required) + *R for Data Science* (free online) - **Both traditions:** you will learn frequentist **and** Bayesian inference — few courses teach both - Submissions happen via Canvas; materials live here # Types of Data & Levels of Measurement {background-color="#1B2A4A"} ## Types of Data **Qualitative (categorical)** - Describe groups or labels (zone, sex, race) - Text / interviews **Quantitative (numerical)** - Measurable amounts (age, prior robberies) - **Discrete** = whole counts (number of robberies) - **Continuous** = can take any value (income, age) ## Levels of Measurement | Level | Definition | Examples | |-------|-----------|----------| | **Nominal** | Categories without order | Race, sex, zone | | **Ordinal** | Ordered categories, unequal gaps | Likert scales | | **Interval** | Meaningful differences, no true zero | Temperature (°C) | | **Ratio** | Meaningful differences **and** true zero | Robbery counts, age | ## Why Does the Level Matter? ::: incremental - Your variable's scale determines **the math you're allowed to do** - It also determines **the plot you should make** - Using the wrong scale leads to **wrong conclusions** ::: ## Scale Determines the Math: Nominal ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # WRONG: the "mean zone" is meaningless rob$zone |> as.numeric() |> mean() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3.17 ``` ::: ::: . . . ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # RIGHT: counts and percentages rob |> count(zone) |> mutate(pct = 100 * n / sum(n)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 3 zone n pct 1 Downtown 32 16 2 East 28 14 3 North 59 29.5 4 South 36 18 5 West 45 22.5 ``` ::: ::: ## Scale Determines the Math: Ordinal ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Summarize a Likert item (ordinal): median & IQR rob |> summarize(med = median(risk_likert), iqr = IQR(risk_likert)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 2 med iqr 1 4 3 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Association with a numeric variable: Spearman (rank-based) cor(rob$risk_likert, rob$prior_robberies_in_zone, method = "spearman") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.001707403 ``` ::: ::: ## Interval vs. Ratio ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mean(rob$temp_c) # ~20 °C ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 20.07643 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mean(rob$temp_c * 1.8 + 32) # same temperatures in °F ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 68.13757 ``` ::: ::: Temperature has **no true zero** — 0 °C is just where water freezes. - "30 °C is 10 °C warmer than 20 °C" ✔ (differences are fine) - "20 °C is *twice as hot* as 10 °C" ✘ (ratios are meaningless) . . . ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mean(rob$age) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 40.605 ``` ::: ::: Age **has** a true zero — a 40-year-old *is* twice as old as a 20-year-old. Differences **and** ratios both work. ## Plots That Match the Scale ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](week-01-stats-is-awesome_files/figure-revealjs/scale-plots-1.png){width=1152} ::: ::: ## Choosing the Right Test (Preview of the Semester) ::: {.cell output-location='fragment'} ```{.r .cell-code} # Categorical × categorical → chi-squared (compare proportions) chisq.test(table(rob$zone, rob$caught)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Pearson's Chi-squared test data: table(rob$zone, rob$caught) X-squared = 2.1521, df = 4, p-value = 0.7078 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell output-location='fragment'} ```{.r .cell-code} # Numeric by category → ANOVA (compare group means) [Session 8] aov(age ~ zone, data = rob) |> summary() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F) zone 4 73 18.15 0.134 0.97 Residuals 195 26419 135.48 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell output-location='fragment'} ```{.r .cell-code} # Numeric × numeric → Pearson correlation [Session 10] cor(rob$age, rob$prior_robberies_in_zone) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -0.004038644 ``` ::: ::: ## Treating Ordinal as Numeric Can Mislead ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} educ <- rep(1:5, each = 50) # ordinal codes 1..5 income <- rep(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 1000), each = 50) # HUGE jump at the top cor(educ, income) # Pearson looks "strong" ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.7088768 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](week-01-stats-is-awesome_files/figure-revealjs/ordinal-trap-plot-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: The correlation is "large," but the categories are **not equally spaced** — code numbers ≠ measurements. # Getting You Running in R {background-color="#73000A"} ## Install R + RStudio (Before Session 2!) Follow the step-by-step guide on the course website: **[smourtgos.github.io/crju705/resources.html](https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/resources.html)** 1. Install **R** (from CRAN) 2. Install **RStudio** (from Posit) 3. Test: type `2 + 2` in the Console → you should see `[1] 4` 4. Install the course packages: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} install.packages(c("tidyverse", "swirl", "BayesFactor", "here")) ``` ::: **Check:** open RStudio and verify you see four panes (Source, Console, Environment/History, Files/Plots/Help). ## First Steps: Arithmetic & Assignment *(Stanton Appendix A)* ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} 3 + 5 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 8 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} x <- 1:10 sum(x); mean(x); sd(x) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 55 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5.5 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3.02765 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ?mean # every function has a help page — use them constantly ``` ::: ## First Steps: Logical Indexing ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x > 5 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} x[x > 5] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 6 7 8 9 10 ``` ::: ::: ## First Steps: Characters & Factors ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} student_names <- c("Alice", "Bob", "Carol") is.character(student_names) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} f <- factor(c("red", "blue", "red")) f ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] red blue red Levels: blue red ``` ::: ::: ::: {.your-turn} **Your turn:** build a vector of seven ages; compute the mean & SD; subset the values > 30; then use `?seq` to generate `seq(0, 1, by = 0.2)`. ::: ## Data Frames & dplyr *(Stanton Appendix B — modern form)* ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) cars_data <- as_tibble(mtcars, rownames = "model") head(cars_data, 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 12 model mpg cyl disp hp drat wt qsec vs am gear carb 1 Mazda RX4 21 6 160 110 3.9 2.62 16.5 0 1 4 4 2 Mazda RX4 W… 21 6 160 110 3.9 2.88 17.0 0 1 4 4 3 Datsun 710 22.8 4 108 93 3.85 2.32 18.6 1 1 4 1 4 Hornet 4 Dr… 21.4 6 258 110 3.08 3.22 19.4 1 0 3 1 ``` ::: ::: ## select & filter ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cars_data |> select(model, mpg, cyl, hp) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 32 × 4 model mpg cyl hp 1 Mazda RX4 21 6 110 2 Mazda RX4 Wag 21 6 110 3 Datsun 710 22.8 4 93 4 Hornet 4 Drive 21.4 6 110 5 Hornet Sportabout 18.7 8 175 6 Valiant 18.1 6 105 # ℹ 26 more rows ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cars_data |> filter(cyl == 6) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 7 × 12 model mpg cyl disp hp drat wt qsec vs am gear carb 1 Mazda RX4 21 6 160 110 3.9 2.62 16.5 0 1 4 4 2 Mazda RX4 W… 21 6 160 110 3.9 2.88 17.0 0 1 4 4 3 Hornet 4 Dr… 21.4 6 258 110 3.08 3.22 19.4 1 0 3 1 4 Valiant 18.1 6 225 105 2.76 3.46 20.2 1 0 3 1 5 Merc 280 19.2 6 168. 123 3.92 3.44 18.3 1 0 4 4 6 Merc 280C 17.8 6 168. 123 3.92 3.44 18.9 1 0 4 4 7 Ferrari Dino 19.7 6 145 175 3.62 2.77 15.5 0 1 5 6 ``` ::: ::: ## mutate & summarize ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cars_data |> mutate(mpg_per_hp = mpg / hp) |> select(model, mpg, hp, mpg_per_hp) |> head(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 4 model mpg hp mpg_per_hp 1 Mazda RX4 21 110 0.191 2 Mazda RX4 Wag 21 110 0.191 3 Datsun 710 22.8 93 0.245 4 Hornet 4 Drive 21.4 110 0.195 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cars_data |> summarize(avg_mpg = mean(mpg), n = n(), .by = cyl) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 3 cyl avg_mpg n 1 6 19.7 7 2 4 26.7 11 3 8 15.1 14 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.your-turn} **Your turn:** using the built-in `mpg` data — (1) find the top-3 models by `hwy`; (2) compute average `cty` by `class`. ::: ## Coming Attractions: Real Data, All Semester Starting next week, our running example is **real**: every crime reported in Chicago in 2025. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](week-01-stats-is-awesome_files/figure-revealjs/chicago-teaser-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Homework (Due Before Noon Tuesday) **swirl tutorials** — interactive R lessons *inside* R: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} install.packages("swirl") library(swirl) swirl() ``` ::: Complete these lessons from *R Programming*: **1)** Basic Building Blocks · **2)** Workspace and Files · **3)** Sequences of Numbers · **4)** Vectors · **5)** Missing Values · **6)** Subsetting Vectors · **7)** Matrices and Data Frames · **8)** Logic · **12)** Looking at Data · **15)** Base Graphics Submit your R script files via **Canvas**. Then read **Stanton Ch. 1** before Session 2.

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
